books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley (August 22, 1862)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862. Public domain. Wording verified against the Collected Works text. “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union, and is not either to save or to destroy slavery. . . . I have here stated my purpose according to my view of official duty; and I intend no modification of my oft-expressed personal wish that all men everywhere could be free.”

—Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Lincoln closes by saying his “personal wish” is that “all men everywhere could be free,” while his official purpose is to save the Union. That split between personal wish and official duty best explains why Lincoln

rationales.A: Background: Lincoln spoke and acted on slavery throughout the war, including the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863.
rationales.B: Background: by August 1862 Lincoln was preparing emancipation as a war measure, not promising to leave slavery alone.
rationales.D: Background: the Emancipation Proclamation opened Union ranks to Black soldiers, and about 180,000 served.
rationales.C: Lincoln kept his personal wish separate from his official duty, so emancipation came step by step, framed as a war measure to save the Union.
rationales.general:
1. Lincoln draws a line inside himself: what he wishes, and what his office allows.
2. The wish is freedom for all; the office is saving the Union.
3. A wish cannot free anyone, but a war measure can.
4. So emancipation arrives dressed as a war measure, one step at a time.
Remember: when a leader splits wish from duty, watch the duty, because that is where the action comes from.
